description: We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about technology, innovation, and problem-solving. We bring together different skills and perspectives in software development, data analysis, artificial intelligence, and creative thinking. Our goal is to collaborate, explore new ideas, and develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges using science and technology. We are eager to learn, share knowledge, and make a positive impact through innovation.
summary:
Smart2Plant is a web tool that helps agronomists in Uruguay plan crop rotations and monitor fields using NASA Earth observation data. The agronomist draws a field and its plots, chooses a crop for each plot, and sees how that plan would perform in a dry, normal and wet year: expected yield, water deficit, soil erosion against the legal tolerance, and pest and frost risk.

The app compares the requested plan with a recommended and a balanced alternative. During the season it tracks each plot by satellite and flags plots whose greenness falls behind what was expected. It also produces reports for farmers and landowners, plus a draft of the Soil Use Plan required by Uruguay’s Ministry of Agriculture.

Today this data is scattered across many portals and formats, and using it takes technical skills most farms lack. Smart2Plant centralizes NASA and local data in one place and shows it in a simple way, answering Field Shift’s call to turn NASA data into farm adaptation decisions. It starts in Uruguay, but the model is built to be replicated in other countries, making crop rotation monitoring and its impact accessible to everyone, at scale.
details:
Smart2Plant is a web tool that helps agronomists plan crop rotations and monitor fields using NASA Earth observation data. The workflow follows the agronomist’s real job in four steps:

  1. Field and plots. The agronomist draws the field and its plots on a satellite map. Each plot gets a profile: slope and low areas from SRTM, soil group from CONEAT, crop suitability from GAEZ, and a likely previous crop from HLS imagery.
    • water balance (Hargreaves evapotranspiration from NASA POWER, rainfall from GPM IMERG, a soil water bucket)
    • expected yield (FAO water-response function)
    • soil erosion (RUSLE) compared with the legal tolerance
    • pest and frost risk
  2. Satellite monitoring. During the season, NDVI from HLS (Landsat + Sentinel-2) is compared with the expected curve for each plot, and plots that fall behind are flagged. A second view compares the field with similar fields nearby.
  3. Reports and sheets. The app produces reports for the farmer and the landowner, editable field sheets, and a draft of the Soil Use Plan required by Uruguay’s Ministry of Agriculture (MGAP).

Benefits

  • One place for the data. Climate, rain, terrain, soil moisture, imagery and soil maps are scattered across many portals and formats; the app brings them together.
  • Easier to understand. It turns raw data into answers an agronomist can act on: which crop, where, and what happens in a bad year.
  • Planning that protects the soil. Erosion is checked against tolerance before sowing, not after.
  • Lower cost. Monitoring uses satellites already in orbit instead of drones or extra field trips.
  • Less paperwork. The Soil Use Plan draft speeds up a procedure that is mandatory for farms with 50 ha or more of crops.

Intended impact

Soil erosion has already reduced productivity on about 30% of Uruguay’s farmland. We want to help agronomists choose rotations that hold up in a dry year and keep soil loss below tolerance. The tool starts in Uruguay, but the NASA layer is global: only the local layer (soil map and national rules) has to change for another country. The goal is to make crop rotation monitoring and its impact accessible at scale, for everyone.

Tools, languages and software

  • Front end: TypeScript, React 19 and Vite, with Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • Maps and visuals: React-Leaflet for maps, @react-three/fiber (three.js) for the 3D field view, Recharts for charts and Framer Motion for animation.
  • Export: jsPDF for PDF reports, the field sheets also export to Word.
  • Data, as designed: the app is designed to use NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SRTM, SMAP, HLS, ECOSTRESS, GLDAS, NASA GIBS/Worldview, FAO GAEZ v4 and MGAP CONEAT. The prototype runs on demo field data shaped like the real outputs; connecting the live data pipeline is our next step. Map imagery currently comes from Esri, with NASA GIBS planned.
  • Other: GitHub for code. We had AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) for code and documents.
  • Hardware: none beyond our own laptops.

What makes it creative

  • Scenario-based results. Every result is shown for a dry, normal and wet year instead of a single forecast, so the agronomist plans for risk, not for the average.
  • Built around a real legal requirement. The Soil Use Plan sits at the center, so the app is useful from the first day.
  • Fills each source’s gaps with the others. Coarse data (SMAP at 9 km, GLDAS at about 25 km) gives regional context, and 30 m HLS and SRTM give detail for each plot.
  • Satellites instead of hardware in the field.
  • A clear visual identity. A 3D field view and our “Your field, connected to space” brand make the data approachable.
  • Alerts on the agronomist’s phone. When a plot falls behind its expected growth, or a weather alert covers one of their fields, the agronomist gets a notification and can act right away instead of waiting for the next visit.

Factors we considered

  • Local fit. MGAP rules (erosion tolerance, the official SGPU submission system) and the CONEAT soil map.
  • Limits of the data. Resolution, cloud cover for optical imagery, and how long each dataset takes to be published (for example, GLDAS arrives about 1.5 to 4 months later). We used each dataset only where it fits.
  • Honesty about the prototype. Four engine values are still fixed assumptions: scenario rainfall and temperature, soil erodibility and tolerance. We listed them and the data that will replace them.
  • Who uses it. The agronomist’s day-to-day workflow, and what farmers, landowners and the ministry each need to receive. We still need to validate this with interviews.
  • Gaps outside NASA data. Crop prices and costs, pest thresholds, and the boundaries of neighbouring fields.
  • Accessibility. The full interface works in Spanish and English, and a free monitoring tier is planned. We designed it so that information never depends on a single channel. Colour always comes with a text label: plot status, scenarios and risk levels say “On plan”, “Dry year” or “High risk” in words, which helps people with colour vision deficiencies and anyone reading a printed report. The next steps are to test the app with screen readers and keyboard-only navigation, check contrast and text size, and make it work well on phones and with the weak connections common in rural areas.
